summary.value:
This paper received three reviews, two with an initial rating of 6 (= marginally above the acceptance threshold), and one with 2 (= reject, not good enough). The authors provided a rebuttal to each of the three reviews, but unfortunately none of the reviewers responded to this rebuttal before the premature end of the discussion period.

The authors further provided a public “Response to Area Chair”, in which they argue that the most negative reviewer (with a rating of 2) significantly misunderstood their paper and made incorrect assumptions.
I find the arguments of the authors in this regard unconvincing. To give one example, the authors mention that this reviewer “repeatedly mentions a unified training setup”, but it is unclear to me what this refers to.
I do not think that the low rating of Reviewer EmKK is due to significant misunderstanding. In fact, many of the concerns this reviewer raises seem well-grounded to me.

As discussed in more detail below, I think it is unlikely that, if there would have been a full discussion phase, the reviewers would have substantially raised their scores. In particular, I expect that reviewer EmKK would still have recommended rejection.

Something else that is important to raise is that some of the results in the paper are presented in a misleading way. In Table 1, all the results with the MePo method are presented in bold, while they are not always the highest (and at other places in the paper, bold results are used to indicate the strongest performance). I strongly urge the authors to be more careful in this regard.

reviewer_concerns.value:
An important concern raised by Reviewer EmKK concerns the limited novelty of the proposed method. In response, the authors explain that their method can be interpreted as an extended pretraining phase. It is however unclear to me how this helps to argue for the novelty of the proposed method, as this appears to me similar to the approach of methods such as MAML and reptile.

I also think the paper’s narrow focus on the Si-Blurry setting, while it is implied that the paper studies “general continual learning”, is an important weakness.

reviewer_scores.value:
An important concern of Reviewer KQGT relates the unclear definitions of offline, online and general CL settings. The authors respond to this concern by saying they revised the section 2.1 of the manuscript to define these terms more clearly. However, only very minor changes were made to this section, and in my opinion, the definition of the terms remains unclear. Moreover, the paper's use of the term "general continual learning" seems unjustified to me. I also find some of the other responses of the authors to concerns of this reviewer underwhelming. I expect that this reviewer would not have raised their rating.

Similarly, I expect that Reviewer jnQ5 also would not have raised their score. For example, this reviewer raised as a weakness that the paper is a bit too empirical, and I do not think the authors convincingly rebut this weakness. The response to this reviewer’s question whether there is evidence of generalization beyond the Si-Blurry setting is in my opinion also not convincing. The authors respond by saying that they added new experiments in various other settings in the Appendix (online, offline and domain CL), but there is almost no description of the experimental details of these new experiments which makes it not possible to critically assess their validity.

As discussed above, an important concern of Reviewer EmKK is the limited novelty of the paper, and I expect that the authors’ rebuttal would not have changed the opinion of this reviewer in this regard. As also discussed above, the authors argue that the reason for the low rating of Reviewer EmKK might be “significant misunderstanding”, but I do not think that this is the case. I expect that Reviewer EmKK would probably not have raised their rating.

summary.value:
This paper studies the setup of general continual learning (GCL) with pretrained models, where the model performs a single pass through a sequence of tasks, with potentially blurred task boundaries. The paper proposes (a) an extended pretraining phase, where the model meta-learns to refine its pretrained representations for improved adaptation to sequential learning, and (b) a method to align the output feature covariance with that from pretraining. The proposed method can be applied on top of existing GCL approaches, and the authors empirically demonstrate its effectiveness on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 task sequences using different pretrained backbones. Ablation studies further show the benefit of each component of the proposed method.

This paper is generally sound, and the proposed method shows convincing performance improvements over baselines. The authors also conduct extensive analyses of their approach. My main concerns are the motivation for the proposed output alignment method and the clarity of certain claims and statements.

strengths.value:
- The proposed method is clean, and the meta-representation learning component is intuitive.
- Extensive experimental analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.value:
1. The arguments made in Sec. 2.2 are not clearly stated; the offline, online, and GCL settings are not defined and the claims in the paragraph starting at L159 lack sufficient evidence. For instance, from Fig. 2b, MVP-Rep appears equally ineffective in both online and offline settings, but the authors state that it does not address online data streams as well. Several claims related to Fig. 2c also seem somewhat overstated, as all methods show similar performance between the online and GCL settings.
2. I find the motivation for output alignment unclear. Specifically, if the data in the incoming batch are drawn from a different distribution than that of pretraining (e.g., imbalanced classes), why should we expect the covariance matrix of their features to match the pretrained one (e.g., balanced classes)? Also, Fig. 4 suggests that pre-aligned features are more separable; but in classification, wouldn’t greater separability generally be desirable?
3. It seems that the pseudo task sequence used in this work always mirrors the structure of the downstream continual learning sequence. In practice, how should such a sequence be constructed during pretraining without knowing the structure of the downstream sequence? It might be useful to analyze the impact of a mismatch between the two.

questions.value:
1. L426: "...due to imbalanced classes." It’s unclear how the performance drop can be attributed to class imbalance without comparing against a balanced setup under otherwise identical conditions.
2. L428: Isn’t this finding contradictory to prior work suggesting that SSL representations are more robust to continual learning than supervised ones [Gal+21, Dav+22]? Could the authors hypothesize why?
3. Fig. 7 shows that MePo produces sparser activations, but *why* are sparser activations desirable?


### Questions/comments that did not impact the score
4. L465: "We empirically validate..." Which specific result does this statement refer to?
5. I wonder if the joint training phase should be considered as the final task in the inner loop, since its only difference from other pseudo-tasks appears to be data composition.
6. The initialization of $\psi$ is not described in the main text but is provided in Algorithm 1 in the Appendix.
7. $\Sigma\text{pre}$ >> $\Sigma_\text{pre}$ in Eq. 8.
8. In Table 1, I recommend either bolding the better method within each of the two rows (w/ vs. w/o MePo) or explicitly reporting the improvement for clarity.

[Gal+21] Self-Supervised Training Enhances Online Continual Learning. Gallardo et al. BMVC 2021.\
[Dav+22] Probing Representation Forgetting in Supervised and Unsupervised Continual Learning. Davari et al. CVPR 2022.

Dear Reviewer KQGT,

We sincerely appreciate your positive feedback on the clarity, design, and depth of our analysis. We have made the following key improvements:

**(1) Clearer definitions and presentation:** We revised Sec. 2.1–2.2 to more explicitly distinguish Offline CL, Online CL, and GCL, and refined the description of Fig. 2. We also clarified the motivation for focusing on self-supervised PTMs, given their prevalence in large-scale foundation models.

**(2) Stronger motivation for Meta-Cov alignment:** We elaborated on why online, imbalanced GCL batches lead to unstable feature covariance and explained how alignment to the stable pretraining covariance mitigates representation drift and bias, ensuring coherent decision boundaries.

**(3) Robustness to pseudo-task mismatch:** We added experiments varying the number of pseudo-tasks \(T'\) across longer GCL sequences (\(T = 10, 20\)), showing that MePo remains consistently effective and scales well across different configurations.

**(4) Clarifications on specific technical points:** We refined explanations regarding the “imbalanced classes” effect in Fig. 5, the behavior of SSL representations in GCL, the benefits of sparse activations, and why OML provides limited gains in pretrained-model settings.

**(5) Implementation clarity:** We clarified the role of the joint-training phase in the outer loop, the definition of \(\phi\), corrected Eq. 8, and improved Table 1 formatting to enhance readability.

We hope you may consider these improvements sufficient for a more positive rating. Feel free to contact us if you have any further question.

Best regards,

The Authors

**Q2: SSL Representations**

The impact of SSL on CL operates at two levels in the context of PTMs. SSL is beneficial mainly during the continual pretraining stage, where contrastive objectives produce flatter minima and robust representations [1-4]. However, self-supervised PTMs often perform worse in downstream CL (continual fine-tuning), especially under parameter-efficient tuning [5-7] (Table 1), because their learned representations are ``too robust'' and thus more difficult to adapt to specific tasks. Although prior work reports strong SSL performance in traditional CL, our results show a different pattern in GCL: self-supervised PTMs such as iBOT lag behind supervised PTMs (Sup-21K) without MePo (Table 1, MISA: 80.35 vs. 65.30 on CIFAR-100). We hypothesize that SSL yields less linearly separable features, making single-pass online adaptation difficult. MePo offers substantial improvements for self-supervised PTMs (65.30 $→$ 75.80) by refining their representations for GCL.

[1] Co2l: Contrastive Continual Learning. ICCV, 2021.
[2] The Challenges of Continuous Self-supervised Learning. ECCV, 2022.
[3] Self-supervised Models are Continual Learners. CVPR, 2022.
[4] Co2l: Contrastive Continual Learning. ICCV, 2021.
[5] Hierarchical Decomposition of Prompt-Based Continual Learning: Rethinking Obscured Sub-optimality, NeurIPS. 2023.
[6] Visual Prompt Tuning. ECCV, 2022.
[7] Improving Visual Prompt Tuning for Self-supervised Vision Transformers. ICML, 2023.

**Q3: Sparse Activation**

Sparser activations are desirable in CL because they reflect reduced representational overlap between classes or tasks, a property shown in prior CL studies [1-4] to lessen interference and mitigate forgetting. We have added more explanations in our revised manuscript (see lines 481-484).

[1] Meta-learning representations for continual learning. NeurIPS, 2019.
[2] Continual semantic segmentation via repulsion-attraction of sparse and disentangled latent representations, ICCV, 2021.
[3] Online task-free continual learning with dynamic sparse distributed memory, ECCV, 2022.
[4] An initial phase decorrelation approach for class incremental learning, ICCV, 2022.

**Q4: Clarify of L465: "We empirically validate..."**

OML [1] introduces meta-learning to CL from scratch, updating the backbone in the inner loop and optimizing a task-specific head in the outer loop. However, when applied directly to our pretrained-model setting, OML achieves only limited improvements: it improves MISA [2] by **only 0.58%** $A_AUC$ on ImageNet-R under Sup-21K, indicating that its design does not effectively exploit pretrained representations for downstream GCL.

Meta-Rep makes two technical innovations that enable substantially stronger results. Instead of meta-learning a classifier head, we meta-refine the pretrained backbone using pseudo sequential tasks from pretraining data, and the outer loop evaluates performance on joint meta-validation data to enforce stability after sequential updates. This CL-tailored meta-objective yields significant benefits, improving MISA by **6.07%** $A_AUC$.


[1] Meta-Learning Representations for Continual Learning. NeurIPS, 2019.

[2] Advancing Prompt-Based Methods for Replay-Independent General Continual Learning. ICLR, 2025.


**Q5: Joint Training Phase**

We would respectfully clarify that the joint training phase is not simply the “final task” in the inner loop. Instead, it is deliberately designed as the meta-objective in the outer loop. Our goal is to ensure that, after learning sequentally arriving pseudo-tasks within the inner-loop, the model can still maintain strong performance on all previously learned pseudo-tasks. This provides a meta-level objective: optimizing the backbone to generate stable representations that are resistant to forgetting.

Conceptually, this formulation serves as an approximation to the second-order gradients commonly used in meta-learning, a technique that has been validated in prior work [1]. Therefore, while the joint training phase differs from the pseudo-tasks only in data composition, its role is fundamentally different: it defines the outer-loop objective for meta-optimization rather than acting as another inner-loop task.

[1] On First-Order Meta-Learning Algorithms. arxiv, 2018 (citation: 3000+)


**Q6: Defination of $phi$**

As described in lines 217, $\phi$ denotes the output layer parameter.

**Q7: Correction of Eq.8**

Thanks. We have revised our manuscript (see lines 280).

**Q8: Presentation of Table 1**

Thanks. We have bolded the better method within each of the two rows (w/ vs. w/o MePo) in our revised manuscript (see Table 1).

We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions. Here we provide a point-to-point response.

**W1: Novelty of MePo**

As shown in CQ1, previos work that employs pretrained models (PTMs) for continual learning (CL) and general CL (GCL) typically adopts a **two-phase paradigm**, i.e., upstream pretraining and downstream CL/GCL. In comparison, our framework expands the upstream pretraining with an additional post-refinement of pretraining data, which is essentially an **extended pretraining phase** tailored to CL/GCL. The key idea lies in pre-adjusting pretrained representations for accommodating dynamic data distributions. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to **prepare PTMs for CL/GCL in advance**, fundamentally different from exisiting PTMs-based CL/GCL methods. 
Following this idea, we propose meta-learning of pseudo task sequences for backbone refinement and meta-covariance for output alignment, which deliever significant performance gains (10-15% in Table 1) over state-of-the-art baselines.

**W2: Theoretical Analysis**

As shown in CQ3, we have added more explanations to analyze how meta-learning of pseudo task sequences enhances downstream CL/GCL, as well as why aligning to the meta covariance matrix benefits the stability–plasticity balance. We have added them in our revised manuscript (see lines 242-250, 318-323).

**W3: Description of "Self-supervised PTM is more realistic":**

We agree that some supervised checkpoints are publicly available. However, we respectfully clarify that current large-scale foundation models are typically pretrained in a self-supervised manner due to the extensive costs of data annotation. As a fundamental research in machine learning, our focus is to highlight the notable challenges of using self-supervised checkpoints for CL/GCL compared to their supervised counterparts. Strategies that perform well on supervised checkpoints may not transfer effectively to self-supervised checkpoints, underscoring the importance and realism of evaluating CL/GCL methods across different PTMs. We have clarified this in our revised manuscript (see lines 162).

**W4: Forgetting Metric**

As described in previous GCL literature [1,2,3], using traditional forgetting metric is usually unfair in GCL due to the presence of blurry and overlapping task boundaries. Consequently, GCL baselines often adopt $A_{AUC}$ and $A_{Last}$ as the evaluation metrics, where obtaining strong $A_{AUC}$ and $A_{Last}$ suggests effective mitigation of catastrophic forgetting. Furthermore, as shown in the responses to CQ2 and your Q2, we have included the forgetting metric for baselines w/ and w/o MePo. The results demonstrate that MePo effectively mitigates forgetting. 
We have added the above results and explanations in our revised manuscript (see Appendix Table 7, lines 789-809).

[1] Online Continual Learning on Class Incremental Blurry Task Configuration with Anytime Inference. ICLR, 2022.

[2] Online Class Incremental Learning on Stochastic Blurry Task Boundary via Mask and Visual Prompt Tuning. ICCV, 2023.

[3] Advancing Prompt-Based Methods for Replay-Independent General Continual Learning. ICLR, 2025.

**W5: throughput of MePo**

As shown in the response to CQ1, MePo does not incurs additional batch time during the downstream GCL phase (see Table 2, 4.84s vs 4.84s).

**W6: Baselines**

We hereby clarify that the results of main baselines are inherited from prior research [1]. According to the authors [1], these baselines have been optimally tuned for the Si-Blurry benchmarks (we have confirmed this via email correspondence with the authors).
Additionally, we conduct all experiments w/ and w/o MePo under identical hyperparameter configurations to ensure fair comparison. We have evaluated MePo against state-of-the-art GCL methods (e.g., MISA and MVP; see Table 1) and additionally provided results under different CL settings (e.g., Offline CL, Online CL, and Domain CL; see the response to CQ2) to further demonstrate its broad applicability. These results indicate that MePo is effective across different benchmark datasets, baseline methods, and CL settings.

[1] Advancing Prompt-Based Methods for Replay-Independent General Continual Learning. ICLR, 2025.


**W7: Description of Algorithm 1**

As shown in the response to CQ1, we respectfully clarify that MePo consists of two distinct stages: the meta post-refinement stage (Algorithm 1, Steps 1–2) and the GCL stage (Algorithm 1, Step 3). In meta post-refinement, we use pretraining data (e.g., ImageNet-K) to refine the backbone and compute the meta covariance. Once this meta post-refinement is completed, the refined backbone and the meta covariance can be seamlessly applied to any downstream CL/GCL methods and datasets, making MePo a plug-in strategy rather than a task-specific modification.

Dear reviewers,

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their effots and valuable suggestions. We are pleased that our work on **Meta Post-Refinement (MePo)** was recognized as tackling a fundamental problem in general continual learning (GCL), with strengths such as being "promising and effective performance" (Reviewers EmKK, KQGT, and jnQ5), "easy to follow and generalist enough to be broadly applicable" (Reviewers EmKK and jnQ5), etc.

Here we summarize following **Common Questions (CQs)**, and also include a point-to-point response to all other questions:

---

**CQ1: Novelty and Computational Cost**

Previos work that employs pretrained models (PTMs) for continual learning (CL) and general CL (GCL) typically employs a **two-phase paradigm**, i.e., upstream pretraining and downstream CL/GCL. In comparison, our approach equips the upstream pretraining with an additional post-refinement using pretraining data, which is essentially an **extended pretraining phase** tailored to CL/GCL. The key idea lies in pre-adjusting pretrained representations for accommodating dynamic data distributions. 
To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to **prepare PTMs for CL/GCL in advance**, fundamentally different from exisiting PTMs-based CL/GCL methods. Following this idea, we propose meta-learning of pseudo task sequences for backbone refinement and meta-covariance for output alignment.

We highlight that the **computational cost** of post-refinement, as an extended pretraining phase, is only **one-time** and is **almost negligiable** compared to the entire pretraining. Thanks to this advance preparation, downstream CL/GCL becomes remarkably **effective and efficient**. Here we provide detailed analyses:

**(1) Post-Refinement (Offline, One-Time Cost):**

The proposed meta learning strategy refines the pretrained backbone in a **method-agnostic and reusable** manner. Once the refined backbone is obtained through pseudo-task sequences constructed from pretraining data, it can be **reused across any downstream CL or GCL sequences without re-running Post-Refinement**. This design aligns with practical deployments, where a single pretrained backbone is repurposed for multiple downstream tasks and scenarios.

Moreover, we find that using only a modest amount of pretraining data and meta epochs is sufficient to obtain strong performance. Specifically, we randomly sample 400 images per class from the pretraining dataset (ImageNet-1K), performing **only 50 epochs** for Sup-21K and **only 10 epochs** for Sup-21/1K to reach convergence. 
The training time is evaluated with three-card 3090 GPU, AMD EPYC 7402 (2.8G Hz):

|Meta Epoch | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | Average |
|----------|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|           |14.43 mins| 14.20 mins| 14.13 mins | 14.00 mins| 13.96 mins| 14.14 mins/epoch | 

In particular, Sup-21K on ImageNt-21K needs to train ~1.3 billion image instances for 90 epochs, but MePo on ImageNt-1K (randomly sampling 400 images per class) only needs to trains additionally ~2 million image instances for 50 epochs, accounting for **only 0.15%** of the entire pretraining.

| Training               | Image Size| Epoch | Batch size | Total Step | Total Images Processed  |
| - | - | - | - | - | - |
| Sup-21K (Pretraining) [1] | 224 x 224 | 90    | 4096       | ~310k      | ~1.3B  |
| Sup-21K (MePo)         | 224 x 224 | 50    | 256        | ~12.8k     | ~2M  | 

[1] An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale. ICLR, 2021.

**(2) GCL (Online, Per-Batch Cost):**

During GCL, the refined backbone ($\theta^*$) is frozen (see Fig. 1). Only lightweight parameters with parameter efficient tuning ($\Delta\theta$) and the output head ($\psi$) are updated. As shown in Table 2, the **GCL phase incurs negligible overhead**, e.g., +0.67% parameters and no additional batch time. 

We have incorporated the above explanations and additional results in our revised manuscript (lines 84-87, 419, 422).

Dear Reviewer jnQ5,

We sincerely thank you for recognizing the strong empirical results, generality, and comprehensive ablations presented in our work. We have made the following key improvements:

**(1) Strengthened theoretical explanation:** We expanded the analysis of MePo’s mechanisms, providing clearer reasoning for how Meta-Rep and Meta-Cov jointly enhance stability–plasticity and overall CL/GCL performance.

**(2) Numerical stability of Cholesky:** We clarified that a small diagonal regularizer ($\epsilon I$) is added to ($\Sigma_{cur}$) to ensure positive definiteness and stable decomposition, and we documented this explicitly in the revision.

**(3) Clarified computational overhead:** We emphasized that MePo functions as a *one-time extended pretraining phase* with modest cost. Once refined, the backbone can be reused across all downstream CL/GCL streams without repeating post-refinement.

**(4) Demonstrated broad generality beyond Si-Blurry:** We added new experiments in Offline CL, Online CL, and Domain CL settings, all showing consistent improvements when integrating MePo. These results confirm MePo’s applicability across diverse CL scenarios.

**(5) Robustness to pretraining data choices:** We provided additional experiments showing that MePo consistently improves performance even when meta-learning is conducted on different datasets (e.g., CIFAR-100 vs. ImageNet-1K). This demonstrates that MePo’s effectiveness does not rely on a specific source dataset.

We hope you may consider these improvements sufficient for a more positive rating. Feel free to contact us if you have any further question.

Best regards,

The Authors

We sincerely thank the reviewers and area chair for their great efforts and constructive feedback.

In our rebuttal, we have tried our best to address all concerns, including:

1. Clarification of definitions and experimental setup. We have clarified the distinction between GCL and other CL settings (online, offline, domain) and added new experiments showcasing MePo's consistent improvements.

2. Data usage and overlap. We have validated that meta-training uses only subsets of pretraining data, with no downstream data, and follows standard CL protocols with disjoint class sets.

3. Computational cost. We have provided runtime analysis showing negligible overhead during GCL and modest, one-time meta-training cost reusable across CL streams.

4. Theoretical analysis. We have explained how each component contributes to mitigating forgetting and enhancing generalization, including Meta-Rep for backbone refinement and Meta-Cov for output alignment.

We believe that the quality of our manuscript has been largely improved. We sincerely appreciate the reviewers' comments again and look forward to contributing to the community.

Best regards,

The Authors

summary.value: The paper proposes a novel method involving meta learning + covariance alignment for real world Continual Learning tasks. This requires them to refine pretrained models first using some "pseudo" tasks, and then simply align the features during online learning. This seems to show 10-15% improvements as a plug-and-play method.

strengths.value:
1. The paper shows strong empirical evidence towards REALISTIC CL scenarios, and is not just constrained to ideal conditions. They also cover multiple datasets / types.
2. The method is generalist enough to be broadly applicable.
3. The ablations are sensible and comprehensive.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper is a bit too empirical - there is no theory regarding why these "pseudo" tasks transfer downstream.
2. There is no numerical stability analysis for the strong distributional assumptions the paper makes.
3. There seems to be substantial overhead to this sort of meta-training - this is not a simple "one-time-cost".
4. The choice of using weighted combination seems a little ad-hoc, and the paper limits itself to the Si-Blurry setting only.

2. What is the performance like without pretraining data availability?
3. What is the numerical stability of the Cholesky decomposition in this setting?
4. Is there evidence of generalization of this method beyond the Si-Blurry setting?

We thank Reviewer KQGT for the positive feedback on our method's clean design and extensive analysis.

**W1: Clarity of Sec. 2.2 and Fig. 2**

Thanks for pointing this out. We have revised our manuscript to define Offline CL, Online CL, and GCL more clearly (see Sec. 2.1, line 127-130). 

For the claim of ``self-supervised PTM is more realistic'', although some supervised checkpoints are publicly available, we argue that most large-scale foundation models are pretrained in a self-supervised manner. As a fundamental research in machine learning, our focus is to highlight the notable challenges of using self-supervised checkpoints for CL/GCL compared to their supervised counterparts. Strategies that perform well on supervised checkpoints may not transfer effectively to self-supervised checkpoints, underscoring the importance and realism of evaluating CL/GCL methods across different PTMs. We have modified the descriptation of Fig.2 in our revised manuscript (see Sec. 2.2, lines 156-164, 170-173).




**W2: Motivation for alignment**

The motivation behind Meta-Cov stems from the inferent challenge of GCL, where online batches are typically small and class-imbalanced, making their feature covariance highly unstable. This instability results in drifting representation geometry, inconsistent class boundaries, and even feature collapse for minority classes, ultimately leading to severe forgetting. In comparison, the pretraining data provides a stable and well-structured covariance matrix $\Sigma_{pre}$ as the reference of pretrained representation space, to which we align the updated feature covariance $\Sigma_{cur}$ in GCL. By applying a Cholesky-based alignment, we constrain online features toward this stable reference, which reduces representation drift, mitigates the bias caused by imbalanced mini-batches (empirically validated in the response to Reviewer EmKK's Q2), and preserves a more coherent representation space (see Fig. 4 and Fig. 6). In this sense, alignment is not an auxiliary or arbitrary addition, but a necessary mechanism for maintaining stable and adaptable representations in GCL.

**W3: Pseudo-task Mismatch** 

We clarify that MePo does not require prior knowledge of the number of downstream tasks. The number of pseudo-tasks ($T'$) used during the post-refinement stage serves as a fixed hyperparameter, and is independent of the downstream GCL task sequence length ($T$). To evaluate the robustness of this design, we conducted experiments under longer GCL task sequences ($T$=10,20) using Sup-21K on ImageNet-R, and tested MePo with varying numbers of pseudo-tasks ($T'$=5,10,20,50). Each setting was repeated 5 times. Results show that MePo remains consistently effective in all settings. Using a longer sequence of pseudo-tasks ($T'$) tends to be more effective when the downstream GCL task sequence is longer ($T=20$ tasks). This validates MePo’s scalability and generality. As shown in the response to CQ1, MePo operates in two stages: post-refinement and GCL. In the post-refinement stage, we refine the backbone by sampling pseudo task sequences from the pretraining data $D_{pre}$, without relying on disjoint or blurry task boundaries. Specifically, as detailed in lines 212, we sample $D_{meta}^{(k)}$ from $D_{pre}$ and split it into $D_{seq}^{(k)}$ (meta-train) and $D_{joint}^{(k)}$ (meta-validation). Once this refined backbone is obtained, it can be directly applied to the downstream CL or GCL $D_t$ with disjoint or blurry task structures. Importantly, the downstream CL or GCL tasks are entirely independent of $D_{pre}$, enabling the refined backbone to generalize effectively across different datasets and CL scenarios (as outlined in CQ1 and CQ2).

**CQ3: Underlying Mechanisms**

Here we provide an in-depth analysis of MePo's underlying mechanisms in improving CL/GCL performance.

**(1) Meta-Rep for Backbone Refinement**

We provide an in-depth theoretical analysis to explain how Meta-Rep improves continual learning performance (lines 972-1079). The key idea is that Meta-Rep minimizes a surrogate meta-objective $\tilde{J}(\theta)$ constructed from pseudo-task sequences sampled from pretraining data. This objective encourages the learned initialization $\theta^\star$ to be robust against gradient interference across tasks.

Specifically, we show that for any two-task sequence $A \rightarrow B$, the deviation between sequential and joint updates is bounded by:
$$
\|\theta_{\mathrm{seq}} - \theta_{\mathrm{joint}}\|
\leq C \cdot \eta^2 \|H_B(\theta)\| \cdot \|\nabla L_A(\theta)\| + \mathcal{O}(\eta^3),
$$
where $H_B$ is the Hessian of task $B$'s loss and $\eta$ is the learning rate. This deviation reflects *catastrophic forgetting* caused by gradient interference. 

Meta-Rep explicitly reduces this bound by learning a $\theta^\star$ with both low curvature and low gradient norm. Under the assumption that pseudo-tasks approximate the downstream distribution, we prove that the forgetting bound at $\theta^\star$ is strictly tighter than that at a generic pretrained initialization. 

This explains why Meta-Rep leads to improved stability–plasticity trade-off and better continual learning performance, as supported by our strong empirical results.


**(2) Meta-Cov for Output Alignment**

Meta-Cov targets a distinct issue in PTMs-based CL: how to properly adapt feature covariance (i.e., an common technique to approximate the structure of representation space) throughout online data streams. Online GCL batches are typically **small, noisy, and class-imbalanced**, causing the empirical covariance matrix $\Sigma_{cur}$ to drift significantly over time. This drift distorts the representation geometry, producing inconsistent decision boundaries and exacerbating interference between tasks.

To counteract this effect, Meta-Cov introduces $\Sigma_{pre}$, a covariance matrix computed from large-scale, balanced pretraining data, which naturally provides a more stable reference geometry. Aligning $\Sigma_{cur}$ toward $\Sigma_{pre}$ via a Cholesky transformation constrains feature updates to remain within a geometrically stable region of the representation space. This operation regularizes unstable directions in $\Sigma_{pre}$, prevents collapse or over-expansion of feature dimensions, and ultimately improves the **balance between stability and plasticity**.

**(3) Empirical Validation**

We have empirically validated the above analyses.
First, the benefits of Meta-Rep tend to be more pronounced when the backbone requires rapid adaptation: self-supervised PTMs perform notably worse than supervised PTMs in GCL, yet MePo significantly improves its performance (e.g., 65.30 to 75.80, performing MISA on iBOT-21K/CIFAR-100, Table 1), consistent with the meta-learning theory that poorly separable representations benefit more from meta-refinement. 
Second, output alignment consistently stabilizes performance under varying batch sizes. Smaller batches produce more volatile covariances, but MePo maintains strong improvements across batch sizes 10, 32, and 64, validating the role of $\Sigma_{pre}$ as a stabilizing reference (see response to Reviewer EmKK's Q2). Finally, representation-level analyses show that the meta-refined backbone exhibits more balanced and better-separated feature distributions (Fig. 6) and sparser activations with reduced overlap (Fig. 7), which alleviates interference and forgetting.

We have added the above analyses and explanations in our revised manuscript (see lines 242-250, 318-323).

Dear Reviewers,

We would like to sincerely thank you for your valuable and insightful comments on our submission. In response to your feedback, we have conducted additional experiments and included the corresponding results to address the raised concerns comprehensively.

We appreciate the time and effort you have devoted to reviewing our work, and we hope that these supplementary materials help clarify and strengthen our contributions. Should you have any further questions or require additional clarifications, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Thank you once again for your consideration.

Best regards,

Authors of MePo

summary.value: This paper proposes meta post-refinement (MePo for rehearsal-free general continual learning. The main ideas of the proposed method are MePo for representation learning and Mepo for feature alignment. The paper is well presented and shows a promising performance as reported in the numerical results. However, the paper has several issues that need to be clarified; please see the weaknesses.

strengths.value:
(1). The paper is presented in a clear yet comprehensive way, and it is easy to follow. 

(2). The numerical results show a promising margin over the existing methods.

weaknesses.value:
(1). From the perspective of methodology, it is questionable whether the paper has enough novelty. Training a base model with meta-learning guidance and feature alignment (combination) by weighted sum is nothing new. I do not see any new/novel mechanisms in either of the ideas.

(2). The proposed method is not supported by theoretical analysis, e.g., how the meta learner helps the base learner to achieve a better stability-plasticity, or how it elevates the base model to achieve a better adaptability to a new task.

(3). It is questionable why "self-supervised PTM is more realistic", while we have free/open supervised PTM models such as pretrained ViT on imagenet-21K or DINO.

(4). Continual learning is the art of defying catastrophic forgetting (CF). But I do not see forgetting measurement and discussion about it. 

(5). GCL that has online learning should be concerned about model throughput (training and inference) as it works on streaming data. Similarly, I do not see measurements and discussion about it.

(6). It is arguably unfair to compare the GCL/Online CL method with offline CL methods such as L2P, DualPrompt,  and CODA-P, especially when you did not search for their best hyperparameter settings in your experiment. Their best parameter setting should be suitable for CL but not for GCL/OCL.  Also, please kindly compare it to the other GCL/OCL SOTAs, i.e., RanPAC[1], RanDumb[2], F-OAL[3], PROL[4], and the newest PEFT (prompt, LoRA, and Adapter) structure.

(7). The pseudo code in Algorithm 1 is not clear on how the model processes each streaming chunk and how the learned knowledge is consolidated from many processed chunks.

Thank you sincerely for your time and service in overseeing our submission, especially under the unusual circumstances caused by the recent OpenReview incident. We deeply appreciate your efforts and commitment to maintaining a fair review process for the ICLR community.

**Summary of Review and Discussion Status**

As detailed in our **Remarks by Authors**, we have submitted a comprehensive rebuttal that thoroughly addresses all reviewer comments. In addition, we have substantially revised the manuscript to reflect the feedback received.

We would like to clarify the review status prior to the Nov 27 identity leak: our submission initially received **two scores of 6** and **one outlier score of 2**. Unfortunately, no reviewers engaged in the discussion phase, and therefore the scores remained unchanged despite our detailed responses.

**Clarifying Key Misunderstandings from Reviewer EmKK**

We respectfully wish to draw your attention to several significant misunderstandings in **Reviewer EmKK**'s comments, which we believe contributed to the anomalously low score.

Many of the reviewer's concerns, particularly those related to the meta-learning mechanism (W2), the computational cost and parameter count (W5, Q3, Q4), and the usage of batch size in evaluation (Q2), appear to stem from **an incorrect assumption** that MePo performs meta-learning jointly on downstream continually arriving data within a single training stage.

However, as emphasized throughout our rebuttal and manuscript, MePo is a **two-stage framework** that explicitly separates (1) **meta post-refinement** using pretraining data, and (2) **general continual learning (GCL)** using only the downstream data.
This distinction is central to the design of MePo. The reviewer’s repeated reference to a unified training setup suggests that they may have misunderstood this foundational aspect of our method. We respectfully hope that this misinterpretation will not unduly affect your independent assessment of the work.

**Final Remarks**

We again thank you for your careful consideration of our submission. Given that (1) the **majority of reviewers gave supportive evaluations** (two confirmed scores of 6), and (2) the **only negative score** appears to be based on a significant misunderstanding of the method, we kindly hope that our rebuttal will be taken into account toward a fair and balanced decision.
